strengths: Clearly identifies and rigorously explains a genuine limitation of CSCNNs (incomplete O(2)-steerable kernel basis due to angular information collapsing in the geometric-product-based kernel network), backed by an explicit symbolic derivation for O(2,0) in Section 3.3 and Appendix A.4.

The proposed fix (conditioning kernels on auxiliary pooled multivector features) is theoretically well-motivated: the paper derives the G-steerability constraint for conditional kernels (Lemma 4.1), proves it is satisfied by the Clifford-steerable conditional kernel construction (Lemma 4.2, Corollary 4.1), and further shows the necessary condition (O(p,q)-equivariance of the pooling operator T) for template-matching efficiency (Proposition 4.1), with full proofs in the appendix.

Extensive empirical evaluation across four physically diverse PDE benchmarks (Navier-Stokes, shallow-water in two settings, 3D Maxwell, and relativistic 2D Maxwell), comparing against 14 baselines including strong recent solvers (Transolver, CViT, LSM, Swin-Transformer, FNO/G-FNO, UNO), with data-efficiency and scaling studies.

Consistent and often large empirical improvements over the original CSCNN baseline across all tasks, and competitive or superior results relative to much larger state-of-the-art models (e.g., matching/exceeding FNO and UNO with far fewer parameters in SWE-5).
Empirical equivariance-error verification (Table 2) supports the theoretical equivariance claims with negligible numerical deviation from the original CSCNN.
Practical, low-overhead implementation via mean pooling for the conditioning operator, keeping the method computationally comparable to the baseline CSCNN.
weaknesses: The title and abstract claim a 'complete kernel basis,' but this is never proven; Conjecture 4.1 explicitly states completeness is unproven, and the supporting evidence (Appendix A.5) is only a symbolic demonstration for the specific O(2,0) case with a hand-picked simple example, not a general argument across p,q or across all missing frequency components. This constitutes an overclaim relative to what is actually established.

The efficient implementation relies on global mean pooling as the conditioning operator T, which is a coarse mean-field approximation; no ablation is provided comparing this design choice to other options mentioned as future work (e.g., local/regional pooling, learnable pooling), leaving the practical necessity/sufficiency of the chosen conditioning largely unvalidated.

No error bars, variance, or multiple-seed results are reported for any of the main experiments (Figures 2, 3, Table 1), making it difficult to assess the statistical significance of the reported (sometimes large, e.g., -53.7%) performance gains.

Some comparisons are not strictly matched (e.g., SWE-5 comparisons across models of very different parameter counts and baselines with results simply taken from another paper), which weakens the strength of the 'on par with SOTA' claims.

The completeness argument and the mechanism by which conditioning restores missing frequency components is demonstrated only via symbolic sympy computation for a toy 2D rotation example, rather than a systematic general proof or broader empirical frequency-recovery analysis (e.g., directly visualizing kernel Fourier content across grades/frequencies for multiple groups).

strengths: Clearly identifies and formally motivates a genuine limitation in CSCNNs—the incompleteness of the steerable kernel basis—backed by a concrete, verifiable O(2,0) example (Example 3.2) showing that vector-vector interactions collapse to angular-frequency-0 only.

Provides a rigorous derivation of the steerability constraint for input-conditioned kernels (Lemma 4.1, 4.2, Corollary 4.1) with full proofs in the appendix, extending implicit parameterization theory to the conditional setting.

Proposes a practical and computationally cheap solution (global mean-pooling conditioning) that preserves translation-equivariant template matching while injecting auxiliary equivariant information into the kernel network.

Reasonably broad empirical validation across four PDE benchmarks (NS, SWE-1, SWE-5, MW3, MW2) against 14+ baselines, with consistent improvements over the CSCNN baseline and competitive performance against state-of-the-art neural PDE solvers (Transolver, CViT, etc.).
Includes an explicit empirical equivariance-error check (Table 2) corroborating the theoretical equivariance claims numerically.
Reasonably detailed implementation and dataset appendices (circular masking for finite-grid equivariance, normalization schemes, hyperparameters) aiding reproducibility.
weaknesses: The paper's title and framing promise a 'Complete Kernel Basis,' but the central completeness claim is only stated as an unproven Conjecture (4.1), supported solely by a narrow symbolic derivation for O(2,0) using sympy code snippets rather than a general proof covering the higher-dimensional and pseudo-Euclidean groups (O(3), O(1,2)) actually used in the experiments; this is a significant gap between the claimed contribution and what is actually established.

The practical conditioning operator T is restricted to global mean pooling, with no ablation of alternative choices (max pooling, learnable/local pooling) despite the paper itself acknowledging these as natural variants; this leaves open whether the specific mean-pooling mechanism is responsible for the gains or whether any extra input-dependent nonlinearity/capacity would suffice.

No ablation isolates whether the performance improvement stems from recovering the theoretically 'missing' steerable degrees of freedom versus simply adding a generic nonlinear, data-dependent modulation to the convolution (e.g., a FiLM-style or non-equivariant conditioning baseline is not tested), making attribution of the gains to the stated theoretical mechanism uncertain.

No variance/seed information or error bars are reported for any of the main results (Figures 2, 3, Table 1), so the statistical significance of the reported improvements (including the large relative gains highlighted in Figure 1) cannot be assessed.
Efficiency claims ('additional computational cost...is negligible') are asserted but not empirically substantiated with wall-clock time, memory, or FLOP comparisons against CSCNN and other baselines.

The connection between the toy completeness argument (Example 4.1, using an arbitrary, position-independent auxiliary multivector) and the actual implementation (global mean-pooled features that are identical across channels/batch at inference) is not rigorously analyzed—e.g., whether pooled features in practice provide sufficiently diverse/generic ζ to realize the claimed frequency components is not verified empirically (e.g., via spectral analysis of learned kernels beyond the single illustrative Figure 1b).

No code release is mentioned, which, combined with the reliance on an unproven conjecture and several implementation-specific design choices (circular masking, grade-wise normalization needed only for MW2), somewhat limits full reproducibility despite the detailed appendix.

strengths: Clearly identifies a genuine, previously acknowledged limitation of CSCNNs (incompleteness of the steerable kernel basis) and proposes a well-motivated remedy by conditioning kernels on auxiliary equivariant input-derived multivectors.

Rigorous theoretical development: the paper derives the generalized steerability constraint for conditional kernels (Lemma 4.1), proves equivariance of the Clifford-steerable conditional kernel (Lemma 4.2) and the corresponding convolution (Corollary 4.1, Proposition 4.1), with full proofs in the appendix.

The worked symbolic example (O(2,0) case, Appendix A.4/A.5, with sympy code) concretely illustrates why single-vector geometric products cannot produce frequency-2 components and how conditioning on an auxiliary multivector restores them, making the abstract claim tangible.

Strong and broad empirical evaluation across four distinct PDE families (Navier-Stokes, shallow-water, 3D and relativistic 2D Maxwell), with 14 baselines, data-efficiency curves, a scaling study (10M to 55M parameters) that remains competitive with much larger models (FNO 270M, UNO 440M), and an explicit numerical equivariance-error check (Table 2) supporting the theoretical equivariance claims.

Practical efficient implementation via mean-pooling-based template matching keeps the added conditioning computationally cheap while preserving parallelism, addressing a real efficiency concern of naively conditioning on pairwise features.
weaknesses: The central 'completeness' claim in the title and abstract is only posed as an unproven conjecture (Conjecture 4.1); it is motivated solely via a special-case symbolic argument for O(2,0) and not established (even informally) for the Minkowski/pseudo-orthogonal groups actually used in the relativistic Maxwell experiments, which weakens the paper's strongest stated contribution.

The practically implemented conditioning (global mean pooling, a mean-field approximation) is a considerable simplification relative to the general theory (which allows conditioning on both sender/receiver features); no ablation studies compare alternative conditioning operators (e.g., local/regional pooling, max pooling), despite these being flagged as important in the Future Work section.

The equivariance-error validation (Table 2) is only reported for E(2); no analogous numerical check is given for the 3D or Minkowski/pseudo-Euclidean settings used in the main experiments, leaving the empirical equivariance validation incomplete relative to the scope of the experiments.

Claims that the additional computational cost of conditioning is 'negligible' are not substantiated with wall-clock or FLOP comparisons, despite being an important practical consideration for adoption.

Parameter-matching rigor is inconsistent across benchmarks (strict matching everywhere except SWE-5, where models of very different sizes are compared), which slightly undercuts the comparability of the scaling results.
Reproducibility details (e.g., whether code will be released) are not explicitly stated, despite reasonably thorough architecture/hyperparameter descriptions in the appendix.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated identification of a real limitation in CSCNNs: the incompleteness of the geometric-product-based implicit kernel basis, illustrated with a concrete, verifiable O(2,0) example (Sec. 3.4) that pinpoints exactly why angular frequency-2 components cannot be generated.

The proposed fix (conditioning kernels on auxiliary multivector features derived from the input) is theoretically grounded: the paper derives the general G-steerability constraint for conditional kernels (Lemma 4.2), proves the resulting Clifford-steerable conditional kernels satisfy it (Lemma 4.3, Cor. 4.4), and shows how translation-invariant conditioning via an equivariant pooling operator T preserves E(p,q)-equivariance while enabling efficient template matching (Prop. 4.5). Proofs are provided in the appendix.

The additional computational overhead of the proposed conditioning (mean pooling) is empirically shown to be negligible (Table 5, <1% inference-time increase over CSCNN), making the method practically attractive.

Extensive empirical validation across four distinct PDE benchmarks (Navier-Stokes, shallow water, 3D Maxwell, relativistic 2D Maxwell) against a large set of baselines (15 total), with consistent and often substantial improvements over the CSCNN baseline (33-54% relative gains reported in Fig. 1c), plus a data-efficiency study, a scaling study, an ablation on the choice of conditioning operator, and an empirical equivariance-error sanity check.

Honest discussion of limitations, including explicitly flagging that the completeness result is only proven for O(2,0) and stated as a conjecture for general O(p,q), and that the current implementation uses a fairly coarse (mean-pooling) conditioning operator.
weaknesses: The central theoretical claim ("completeness of the kernel basis") is proven only for the O(2,0) case; for general pseudo-Euclidean groups it remains an unproven conjecture (Conjecture 4.7), which the paper itself acknowledges is "highly non-trivial" to establish. This leaves the main advertised theoretical contribution incomplete and reliant on empirical evidence from a fairly narrow set of tasks.

The practical instantiation of the general conditional-convolution framework (Def. 4.1, which allows arbitrary pointwise conditioning on f(x), f(y)) is reduced in practice to conditioning on a single global, translation-invariant mean-pooled multivector (Eq. 16). This is a substantial simplification relative to the general theory, and it is unclear how much of the richer message-passing-like expressivity implied by Def. 4.1 is actually being exploited versus a much simpler global feature injection; the paper does not explore intermediate options (e.g., local/windowed pooling) in the main text, only briefly noting it as future work.

On the electrodynamics tasks (MW2, MW3), the non-equivariant Transolver baseline outperforms C-CSCNN, and on SWE-5, larger non-equivariant models (CViT-L, U-F2Net) outperform the scaled C-CSCNN despite comparable or larger parameter budgets. This tempers the significance claim of consistently state-of-the-art performance and raises open questions about when the equivariance bias is actually advantageous versus when richer non-equivariant architectures dominate.

The empirical equivariance-error check (Sec 5.3, Eq. 18) is only performed for a single convolutional layer on one dataset (NS) and does not verify equivariance of the full multi-layer, non-linear network used in the actual experiments, which is the setting where equivariance guarantees are practically most relevant.

Some experimental comparisons are not fully controlled: for SWE-5, baselines and the proposed model differ substantially in parameter count (Table 2) rather than being parameter-matched as in other tasks, complicating direct interpretation of the scaling claims.
The paper does not clearly state whether code/data will be released, which affects reproducibility despite detailed appendix descriptions of architectures and hyperparameters.

strengths: Identifies and clearly demonstrates a real theoretical limitation of CSCNNs (incompleteness of the implicit kernel basis for vector-vector interactions, worked out explicitly for O(2,0) via a geometric-product argument and symbolic computation).

Provides a full chain of equivariance proofs (Lemmas 4.2, 4.3, Proposition 4.5, Corollary 4.4) for the proposed conditional convolution and conditional Clifford-steerable kernels, which is a non-trivial and mathematically careful contribution.

Broad empirical evaluation across four PDE benchmarks (Navier-Stokes, shallow-water, 3D Maxwell, relativistic 2D Maxwell) against a large set of 15 baselines, including data-efficiency curves, a scaling study, an equivariance-error sanity check, and an ablation over conditioning operators (mean/max pooling vs. non-equivariant random conditioning).

The efficient 'template matching' formulation (conditioning on a translation-invariant pooled field rather than full pairwise features) is a sensible practical compromise between expressivity and computational tractability, and is shown to add negligible inference overhead over standard CSCNNs.
Writing in the theoretical sections (Sec. 3-4) is precise and the running O(2,0) example is pedagogically useful for understanding why the base method is incomplete and why conditioning helps.
weaknesses: The paper's central theoretical claim -- that conditioning restores completeness of the kernel basis for general pseudo-Euclidean groups O(p,q) -- is left as an unproven conjecture (4.7), supported only by a worked example for the compact O(2,0) case. Given that the title and abstract emphasize 'arbitrary pseudo-Euclidean groups,' this is a significant gap between the claimed scope and the actual evidence provided.

The empirical 'on par with SOTA' claim is overstated: Transolver (a non-equivariant, generic PDE transformer) clearly and consistently beats C-CSCNN on both electrodynamics tasks (MW3, MW2) at every training-set size in Table 1, and in the scaling study (Table 2) CViT-L (92M) and U-F2Net (344M) outperform the larger C-CSCNN (55M) by a sizeable margin. The abstract's framing undersells these losses.

The chosen conditioning operator (global mean pooling over the whole spatial field) is a fairly coarse, non-local, data-independent summary; it is unclear how this generalizes to heterogeneous domains, large grids, or problems with spatially varying statistics, and the ablation only compares it against max-pooling and a non-equivariant random baseline rather than more informative locally-varying conditioning alternatives, leaving the core design choice weakly justified beyond this specific benchmark suite.

Computational cost analysis is relegated to the appendix and shows C-CSCNN is substantially slower than Transolver (54.3ms vs 39.1ms) and ~30x slower than a plain ResNet, which somewhat undercuts the practical appeal of the method relative to the strongest baseline it is being compared against; this trade-off deserves more prominent discussion in the main text.

One of the four benchmark tasks (relativistic 2D Maxwell) uses a custom-generated dataset with several heuristic normalization and filtering choices (log-Minkowski-norm scaling, ad hoc outlier removal); no code or data release is mentioned, raising reproducibility concerns for this non-standard benchmark.

The novelty of the core idea (conditioning/input-dependent steerable kernels) is incremental relative to prior work already cited in the paper (e.g., relaxed/non-stationary equivariant kernels, message-passing-style point convolutions with sender/receiver conditioning); the main new element is applying this idea within the Clifford-steerable CNN framework and deriving the corresponding constraint, which, while valid, is a narrower contribution than the framing suggests.

strengths: Clearly diagnoses a concrete, previously under-examined limitation of Clifford-Steerable CNNs (incompleteness of the implicit kernel basis), with a rigorous worked example for O(2,0) showing exactly which angular frequency components are missing and why (Sec. 3.4, Appendix A.4).

The proposed fix (conditioning kernels on auxiliary equivariant features derived from the input field) is theoretically grounded: the paper derives the general steerability constraint for conditional kernels (Lemma 4.2), proves that the Clifford-steerable conditional kernel satisfies it (Lemma 4.3), and proves equivariance of the practical template-matching implementation via an equivariant pooling operator T (Prop 4.5), with full proofs in the appendix.

Extensive empirical validation across four distinct PDE tasks spanning different symmetry groups (O(2,0), O(3,0), O(1,2)) and against 15 baselines, including strong recent neural PDE solvers (Transolver, CViT, FNO/G-FNO, UNO, Swin-Transformer, LSM).

Multiple complementary analyses: data-efficiency curves (Fig. 2, Table 1), parameter-scaling study (Table 2), an ablation on choice of conditioning operator (Appendix D.1) justifying the mean-pooling design choice, numerically measured equivariance error confirming the theoretical claims are respected in practice, and reported inference overhead showing the method is nearly as fast as standard CSCNN.

Honest and specific limitations section, explicitly flagging that the general completeness claim (Conjecture 4.7) is unproven, that only simple conditioning operators were explored, and that discretization breaks exact equivariance — these are not glossed over.
The paper is well organized, clearly written, and builds logically from theoretical background to the proposed method to experiments, making the technical contribution easy to follow.
weaknesses: The central theoretical claim motivating the method's generality — that conditional kernels restore completeness for arbitrary O(p,q) — remains an unproven conjecture (4.7); the only rigorous demonstration is for the O(2,0) case, so the paper's broader completeness claims rest on empirical performance gains rather than proof for the general pseudo-Euclidean setting.

Despite the title's and abstract's framing of being 'on par with state-of-the-art,' the method is actually second-best (behind Transolver) on both electrodynamics tasks (MW2, MW3) and is outperformed by CViT-L and U-F2Net on the SWE-5 scaling benchmark, which is a non-equivariant, much larger model; this nuance could be stated more carefully in the abstract/introduction rather than only in the body text.

The practical implementation relies on a very coarse conditioning signal (global mean/max pooling over the whole domain), which sacrifices most of the expressivity promised by the general conditional convolution theory (Def 4.1) in exchange for parameter sharing/efficiency; the paper acknowledges this but does not explore intermediate options (e.g., local/regional pooling) despite proposing them as future work, leaving a gap between the theoretical framework and what is actually validated.

All experiments are conducted on regular grid-based PDE benchmarks; despite claims of broader applicability to point clouds, robotics, and computer vision, no experiments test the approach outside structured grid settings, so the generality of the contribution beyond PDE forecasting on grids is unverified.

Only inference time is reported (for one task); training-time/computational overhead comparisons across all tasks and baselines are missing, which would help assess practical cost-benefit given the conditioning mechanism and Clifford algebra operations are noted to be unoptimized.

The equivariance error comparison (CSCNN: 2.4e-7 vs C-CSCNN: 3.4e-7) is reported for only a single task without statistical variance or broader group coverage, offering fairly thin empirical support for the equivariance claims relative to the theoretical rigor elsewhere in the paper.
